video_title: Rational Security: The "Snifting Up to Boston" Edition
gist: Lawfare's Rational Security panel (Scott R. Anderson, Benjamin Wittes, Ari Tabatabai, Joel Braunold) covers three international flashpoints. First, Israel's October 27 election looks set for deadlock and weeks of coalition maneuvering, with Netanyahu weakened, Trump's endorsement worth little, and a looming fight over the final $3.3B year of the US-Israel MOU if Democrats take the House. Second, a sharp Trump-Zelensky rupture: the Russian diesel sanctions deal, withheld interceptors and Starlink disruptions push Ukraine toward Congress and Europe. Third, France's biggest unrest since 1968, which is boosting Le Pen ahead of 2027. (The title is a joke from the cold open and has nothing to do with the content.)

insights.claim: Ahead of Israel's October 27 election, no mainstream poll has shown Netanyahu's coalition bloc reaching the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern; only Channel 14 and i24-linked pollsters with questioned methodology show it passing 61.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Base case is no clean Netanyahu majority; discount outlier polls from right-leaning outlets.
insights.quote: there's not been one poll since polling really started going in this election that showed that block getting 61 seats

insights.claim: The Jewish opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot's party polls at roughly 55-58 seats; counting Arab parties the anti-Netanyahu camp is about 75 of 120, but Bennett, Lieberman and (inconsistently) Eisenkot refuse to govern with Arab parties, leaving ~105 seats to fight over for 61.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: A large anti-Netanyahu majority may still fail to form a government because of self-imposed boycotts, raising odds of deadlock.

insights.claim: Because Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold discards votes for parties that fall short (roughly 160,000 votes per party), a few thousand votes for two threshold-hugging parties (Ofer Vinter's right-wing party and the Reservists and Economics Party) could decide whether the opposition reaches 61, and poll samples of 500-700 cannot resolve this.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Polls are structurally unable to call this election; expect high outcome variance and avoid positioning on poll leads.
insights.quote: if you vote for a party that doesn't make 3.25, your votes literally go in the trash

insights.claim: If the four main opposition parties hit about 58 seats on election night, expect them to try a minority government that replaces the Knesset speaker, establishes a state commission of inquiry into October 7th, passes a law barring an indicted PM from serving, then forces new elections aimed at a Likud-without-Netanyahu coalition.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Netanyahu's exit could come even without a 61-seat opposition win, via a minority-government sequence.

insights.claim: Both Likud and Eisenkot are running 'largest party' campaigns, cannibalizing votes within their own blocs to win the presidential mandate to try forming a government first, signaling both have effectively given up on winning their blocs outright.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Signals a fragmented post-election negotiation rather than a decisive result.

insights.claim: The outcome of Israel's coalition formation probably will not be known until 3-4 weeks after the election, as it hinges on whether parties really mean their refusals to work with Mansour Abbas and the ultra-Orthodox.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Expect weeks of political uncertainty in Israel after October 27, not an election-night resolution.

insights.claim: Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox parties may not stick with a weakened Netanyahu because their youth are being arrested as criminals for not serving in the army, and their leadership's sole demand is fixing that; they will give loyalty to whoever does.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: The draft issue is a swing lever that could split Netanyahu's coalition.

insights.claim: Israeli politics has four or five overlapping fault lines (hawk/dove security left-right, Jewish/Arab, religious/secular, religious-nationalist vs ultra-Orthodox, and 'Bibi or not Bibi'), and the election tests whether anti-Netanyahu sentiment can override all the others.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Useful lens for judging whether any anti-Netanyahu government would be stable or quickly fracture.

themes.theme: Netanyahu's messaging and the fading Trump effect

insights.claim: The opposition attacks Netanyahu on four lines: October 7th accountability, siding with the ultra-Orthodox on the draft, judicial reform threatening Israel's future and high-tech economy, and West Bank violence from failing to restrain the far right of his coalition.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Judicial reform's linkage to the high-tech economy remains a live political risk factor for Israeli tech.

insights.claim: Netanyahu's core pitch is 'it's either me or Palestine': he frames Israel's diplomatic isolation and looming economic pressure as inevitable forces only he can withstand, after the next two years of Trump.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: A Netanyahu win implies continued confrontation and isolation; it is a compelling message to his base.
insights.quote: Netanyahu is basically saying, "It's either me or Palestine."

insights.claim: Pro-Israel US commentators (including FDD voices) warn that the economic warfare used against Iran could be turned on Israel, built by Democrats, which reflects a growing boycott and isolation risk for the Israeli economy.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Signals tail risk of sanctions-style pressure on Israel under future Democratic control.

insights.claim: Trump's popularity in Israel collapsed after his MOU with Iran in June, which Israelis saw as betrayal (including being forced to halt operations in Lebanon), so his 'complete and total' endorsement of Netanyahu carries very little weight with voters.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: US leverage over Israeli voters is weaker than headlines suggest; do not overweight the endorsement.

insights.claim: Netanyahu himself is publicly signaling Israel has two more years of freedom under Trump before it gets squeezed, implying an incentive to lock in maximal regional gains before 2029.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Expect Israeli policy to front-load aggressive moves within the Trump window.
insights.quote: We've got two more years of freedom and then we're screwed.

insights.claim: Netanyahu deliberately shifted Israel from seeking bipartisan US support to an alliance with one US party and Orthodox American Jews (about 20% of US Jews), creating serious exposure when US political leadership changes.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Raises structural risk to US-Israel aid and diplomatic backing under a future Democratic government.

insights.claim: If Democrats win the House in the midterms, there will not be the 218 votes to appropriate the 10th and final year of the US-Israel MOU's $3.3 billion, forcing either continuing resolutions or a funding fight, and any new Israeli government will have to negotiate with the House speaker as well as the White House.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Concrete risk to US military financing for Israel (and related defense contractor flows) starting January.
insights.quote: there are not 218 votes. they just don't exist

insights.claim: The shift away from deference to Israel is generational and will persist regardless of whether Netanyahu wins, extending from Democrats and DSA candidates to the restraint wing of the Republican Party; Biden was the last to embody the traditional approach.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: US support for Israel is on a secular decline; position for lower long-run aid and higher conditionality.

insights.claim: A new non-Netanyahu prime minister would create some optionality in US relations, but if the current coalition with Smotrich and Ben Gvir returns, with Smotrich campaigning on Palestinian emigration, there is no hope of repair.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Election outcome is the key binary for the trajectory of US-Israel relations.

insights.claim: In the lame-duck period between the US midterms and the new Congress, expect a Trump-Netanyahu push to escalate against Iran and 'finish the job', which Trump has already signaled.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Elevated risk of Iran escalation, and oil and shipping disruption, in roughly November-January.

insights.claim: Trump has eased US sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a mostly symbolic move that may not affect oil prices but aligns Trump's domestic political interest in lower fuel prices with Putin's economic interests and war effort.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief on Russian energy is being driven by US pump-price politics rather than market fundamentals.

insights.claim: High oil and diesel prices are driven by the Strait of Hormuz being barely open and Bab el-Mandeb disruptions from the Iran war, not Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries; Russian diesel has long been a minor factor in the global market.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Energy prices should be tracked against Gulf shipping, not Ukraine-Russia refinery strikes or Russian sanctions relief.

insights.claim: The administration has held up delivery of missile interceptors already paid for by European countries and interrupted Starlink/Starshield service that Ukraine depends on for drone guidance, and intelligence sharing on Russian missile launches may also have been cut, which signals Ukraine can be cut off at any time.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Shows key-vendor and supplier dependency risk (SpaceX, US interceptor supply) for Ukraine and European buyers of US arms.

insights.claim: The real damage is unpredictability itself: US oscillation eases pressure on Russia to negotiate while weakening the reassurance that Ukraine and NATO need, which plays into Russia's hands whether or not this moment is a turning point.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Volatility in US policy is a persistent risk premium for European security and defense planning.
insights.quote: what Ukraine needs right now is consistency and predictability

insights.claim: Republican members of Congress at the Warsaw Security Conference told Ukrainians to ignore White House statements and claimed the diesel deal would not go through, and the audience laughed at claims Trump supports the Graham Act sanctions.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Congressional reassurances lack credibility; do not price in sanctions enforcement via Congress.

insights.claim: Trump is appeasing Putin partly out of fear that Russia will step up intel sharing and military support to Iran, which would further tie US hands in a war he sees as going badly.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Links the Ukraine and Iran theaters; Russian leverage over the US rises as the Iran war drags on.

insights.claim: Zelensky has abandoned his post-Oval-Office strategy of avoiding being seen as the problem party: Ukraine resumed long-range strikes on Russian energy after about 72 hours when Russia did not reciprocate, and is leaning openly on European backers.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Expect continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure regardless of US pressure.

insights.claim: Ukraine's pro-Republican support base is thinning: Mitch McConnell, Joni Ernst and others are leaving the Senate and few Ukraine sympathizers remain in the White House, while Vice President Vance is openly antagonistic.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Fewer GOP champions means weaker legislative support for Ukraine aid under Republican control.

insights.claim: Ukraine's optimal strategy is to diversify: keep tactical intel and staff-level DoD/CIA ties with the Trump administration while dealing with each European country, NATO, and Congress directly, building a bipartisan congressional base as Israel did against less friendly executives.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Points to Congress-driven Ukraine funding as the key variable after the midterms.

insights.claim: Ukraine still commands rare supermajorities in Congress, potentially 75 senators and 300-plus House members, which Zelensky tapped by holding a conference call directly with a bipartisan group of lawmakers, bypassing the president.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Gives a credible path for appropriations to force aid on an unwilling executive.

insights.claim: Democrats do not yet have a coherent post-Trump foreign policy vision for the Middle East, Russia-Ukraine or China; they know what they oppose (paying for wars seen as unwinnable), and being too pro-Ukraine risks being read as Biden nostalgia.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Policy after 2028 is highly uncertain; do not assume a return to the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus.

insights.claim: Ukraine support fares better as a quiet, insider appropriations issue; the more it becomes a high-profile presidential-campaign topic, the worse for Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Watch whether Ukraine aid stays technocratic or becomes a 2028 campaign wedge.

insights.claim: Trump treats the next two years as his only window to 'finish' Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, believing history ends when he leaves office, which creates dangerous pressure for rushed, reversible deals and sudden flips between allies and enemies.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Expect elevated geopolitical volatility and abrupt policy reversals through 2028.

insights.claim: France's protests, the largest since 1968, began over underfunded public education and broadened into a cost-of-living revolt; more than 1,500 businesses have been damaged or destroyed, from luxury brands like Chanel and Hermes to small shops, with roughly 1,800 arrests.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Direct hits to French retail and luxury storefronts, plus temporary unemployment costing hundreds of millions of euros.

insights.claim: Macron's televised address fell flat, his interior minister offered to resign (refused), and he then left for Gulf visits to Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE to negotiate lower gas prices while parts of the country were still burning; more protests are expected this Saturday.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: French political instability and energy-price diplomacy with Gulf suppliers are both escalating.

insights.claim: French politics is converging on a far-right (Marine Le Pen's National Rally, the front-runner) versus far-left (Melenchon) choice as the center has discredited itself after years of failing to fix the economy, the safety net and a large debt and deficit.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Rising odds of a non-centrist French president in spring 2027, with implications for French fiscal policy and spreads.

insights.claim: Protest is a built-in feature of the French political bargain (a centralized, bureaucratic state in exchange for the right to riot), so the unrest is not nihilism; if the far left cannot separate itself from the violence, moderate candidates could still reach the runoff and win.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Argues against assuming an extremist victory in 2027 is inevitable.

insights.claim: In the UK, Andy Burnham has become prime minister and stabilized Labour by beating the far right in his own by-election and the Greens in the former prime minister's seat, evidence that populist momentum does not necessarily compound.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: A precedent suggesting European centrist parties can recover from populist surges.
